questions.question: What does the Weierstrass Approximation Theorem guarantee for a continuous $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$?
options: For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, there is a polynomial $P$ with $\|P-f\|_\infty \lt \varepsilon$.
For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, there is a linear function $P$ equal to $f$ everywhere.
Every continuous function on $[a,b]$ is itself a polynomial.

options: No polynomial can approximate $\mathrm{e}^{x}$ on a closed interval.
The theorem applies only to constant functions.

questions.question: What does it mean that polynomials are dense in $C^0([a,b])$ with respect to the uniform norm?

questions.question: Which claim is stronger than the Weierstrass approximation theorem actually gives?
options: Every continuous function on $[a,b]$ can be uniformly approximated by polynomials.

Every continuous function on $[a,b]$ is equal to one polynomial on all of $[a,b]$.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to apply the Weierstrass approximation theorem to $f(x) = \mathrm{e}^{x}$ over all of $\mathbb{R}$?
options: The uniform norm is never used for approximation.

Given any discontinuous function on $[a,b]$, approximate it uniformly by a constant exactly.
Given a polynomial $P$, conclude every continuous function equals $P$.
